units: a neighbor reports that his printing machine was damaging the paper
the user had tried rough handling without getting any result
a local repairman blames the fault on a worn drive belt
the belt had lost its grip from turning with no load
the repairman advises reaching the back part of the device
a round part must be turned one notch to tighten the belt again
the device pulls the paper properly after the operation
the owner had thought of throwing out a machine that could be fixed
he decides to keep the instructions within reach
text: A neighbor across the street told me his printer kept pulling sheets in crooked and creasing every one of them. He had shaken it, thumped it, yanked at the tray, and all he ever got was another jam. Then a repairman down the street set him straight: the drive belt had gone smooth from spinning with nothing to grip, so it slipped instead of pulling. Open the back panel, the man said, find the little wheel sitting on the side, and turn it one notch to take up the slack. My neighbor grumbled the whole time, but he called me the next morning sounding almost cheerful, because the paper was finally feeding in straight. He laughed about it later. He had nearly thrown out a working machine over a stretched piece of rubber, and from now on the manual stays in the drawer where he can reach it.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: two ways of sending messages far off existed side by side for a long period
the first method used tall towers carrying movable arms
one worker set the arms and another read the shape through a telescope
the second method sent a current through an insulated metal wire
this wire was buried along the roads or hung from posts
mist and darkness cut off the working of the arm device
the wire worked without depending on the weather
the chain of towers took a large staff to run
the electric line kept only one worker busy at each of its ends
the price of the cable held back the spread of the second method
text: For a long stretch of years, two ways of throwing a message across country ran side by side. The older one built tall towers up on the ridges, each crowned with jointed wooden arms that an operator swung into shape on command, while a second man at the next tower read that shape through a telescope and passed it on down the chain. The other pushed a current along a metal wire sheathed in insulation, buried beside the roads or strung up from posts. The towers went blind the moment the mist rose or the daylight failed. The wire, for its part, never cared in the least what the sky happened to be doing. Keeping the chain alive took whole crews of watchful operators, while the electric line needed one man at each end and nobody at all in between. What held the wire back was the price of the cable, which slowed its spread for a long while yet.

units: the machine described builds an object by stacking layers of matter
its bulk is close to that of a piece of luggage
a spool carries a plastic thread that unwinds toward the machine
a heated tip softens this thread and lays it down in thin ribbons
a moving support drops a little at every pass of the tip
the object is therefore built from the bottom upward
a blower cools the fresh matter to keep it from sagging
an electronic board rules the movements of the whole assembly
the device is light enough to stand on a household table
text: A machine that lays matter down layer by layer fits inside a box hardly wider than a suitcase. Look first at the spool, where a translucent plastic thread lies coiled like patient rope and feeds inward slowly, without hurry. Next comes the nozzle, a heated point that softens the thread and sets it down again in thin ribbons, still faintly warm to the touch. Beneath it the bed slides along and drops by a hair with every pass, so that the object grows upward as it takes shape. A small fan breathes on the fresh ribbon and sets it firm before it has time to slump. Last of all, tucked away under the frame, an electronic board counts the pulses and rules every movement. None of it weighs much at all. The whole thing stands on an ordinary kitchen table and hums away like a diligent insect.

units: a crew raised a mast on the roof of a technical building
the part put up is a hollow cylinder made of a light metal
it took the place of a device that vibration had cracked
the fitters bolted the base down onto a thick metal plate
they checked that it stood upright before the final tightening
a rising wind set the mast humming on a steady note
the supervisor stopped the work and measured the frequency
the structure was resonating with the gusts
fitting two diagonal stays moved the natural frequency
the closing readings confirmed the performance expected
text: Work started well before first light, when the crew hauled the mast sections onto the flat roof of the technical building. The antenna itself was a hollow cylinder of light alloy, brought in to replace an older one that vibration had cracked. The fitters bolted the base down flat onto a thick steel plate, then checked it against a plumb line before they took the nuts up tight. By midday the wind had picked up and the mast began to hum on a low, steady, unsettling note. The supervisor called a halt, measured the frequency, and saw that the structure was resonating with the gusts. Two extra stays went on at an angle, which shifted the natural frequency well clear of the danger band. The cable was landed at dusk, and the closing readings confirmed the gain that everyone had been promised.

units: the power must be cut and the machine left to cool before any work
a hot liquid swells and may spurt out when the fitting is opened
a container has to be set under the lower coupling
the draining is done by the weight of the liquid alone
the valve must be opened by a quarter turn and no more
opening too fast draws in air and the flow stops
the bleed control at the top lets air enter from above
the refill is done through the upper port once the valve is shut
filling little by little keeps bubbles from forming
a circuit without bubbles carries heat at a steady rate
text: Before you touch the cooling circuit at all, unplug the machine and let it cool down. Hot water swells, and the pressure it builds up in the flexible hose will send the liquid spitting out the moment a fitting comes loose. Set a pan under the lower coupling next, since the draining is done by weight alone and nothing else. Open the valve a quarter turn and no more. Cracked open too quickly, it draws air in, the flow stalls, and the whole job comes to nothing. Now drop the bleed lever at the top of the circuit, so that air enters from above and drives the liquid downward. Once the pan stops filling, shut the valve, wipe the coupling dry, and top the circuit up through the upper port. Fill little by little to keep bubbles out, and a circuit without bubbles carries heat at a steady rate.

units: a volunteer group takes in broken devices every week
the place used is a covered hall lent by the neighborhood
most of the objects have a fault of small scale
the faults named are a soldered battery a corroded contact or a glued shell
the makers explain these joins by sealing and slimness
the repairers read them as a deliberate cut in how long a product lasts
the workshop records every opening in a logbook and in pictures
the sheets produced are handed out freely
a partner supplier sends over batches of standard contacts
most of the devices brought in leave again in working order
text: Under a covered hall lent by the neighborhood, a volunteer group takes in broken machines and discouraged owners week after week. What the volunteers keep finding is small: a battery soldered into place, a corroded contact, a shell glued shut that no ordinary tool opens without cracking it apart. Manufacturers point to sealing and slimness to explain these permanent joins, while the repairers read them instead as a way of cutting short how long a product lasts. So the workshop has answered with a method of its own. It keeps a logbook of every model it has opened, photographs each step, and hands the resulting sheets out for anyone at all to use. A parts supplier has joined in with them and now sends over batches of standard contacts. Since this season, two machines in three walk back out working.

units: two speakers are looked at side by side
the first is a cube of very light plastic
its grille copies the look of metal
the second has a shell of folded metal and weighs more
a stretched cloth covers the front of the second one
the cube lacks strength in the low sounds
the heavier one holds the low notes without shaking
the cube travels easily and takes knocks
the second one needs a wall socket and a steady surface
the choice comes down to what the speaker will be used for
text: Stand the two speakers next to each other and you see the difference before anything is plugged in. The first is a molded plastic cube, light as an empty box, with a printed grille that pretends to be metal. The second has weight in the hand: folded sheet metal, edges turned over, and a stretched cloth across the front that hints at a real cone behind it. Listen, and the cube snaps in the treble but runs out of breath as soon as the bass drops. Its heavier neighbor holds the note, fills the whole room, and barely shivers on the shelf. The other side of the ledger counts for something too. The cube slips into a bag, charges overnight, and shrugs off knocks, while the big one wants a wall socket and a steady corner. Each has its own ground, and what you plan to do with it settles the argument.

units: the writer argues against the praise given to thin devices
the first complaint bears on the battery held down with adhesive
a glued battery dooms the object as soon as the charge fades
the second complaint targets screws with an exclusive head
these screws keep independent shops away from repair work
the third complaint concerns software that turns away an unpaired part
the three obstacles strengthen one another
the writer grants that shrinking a case forces trade-offs
he asks that the buyer be told before the purchase
text: We ought to stop praising a thin device as though slimness were a moral achievement. The case against it comes in three parts. Take the glue first: bonding a battery to the frame does the owner no good at all, and it dooms the whole object the day the charge starts to fade. Then the odd screw, cut with a head that no common driver will grip, whose only job is to keep the independent shop out of the work. Then the software, which turns away a spare part identical in every respect because the factory never paired it to the machine. The three locks feed one another. The glue makes opening risky, the screw makes it awkward, the software makes it pointless. Yes, shrinking a case forces trade-offs, and that much is true. The buyer should hear about them at the counter, not the day after the breakdown.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: as a child she took apart the clocks in her house
she rarely put them back together in full
her training took place in a mechanics workshop
that workshop repaired lifting machinery
her first job was greasing the grooved wheels
she watched how metal tires and how a groove wears away
once she became a technician she went down into the pit alone
she carried a hand crank for emergencies at her belt
she was later handed the diagnoses her colleagues had given up on
she now passes her trade on to apprentices
text: As a child she pulled apart every clock in the house to see what was ticking inside, and rarely got one whole again. As a teenager she took an apprenticeship in a mechanics workshop that repaired hoists. Her first job was a thankless one: greasing pulleys, one after another, until the cable ran without a squeal. What she learned there was how matter tires, how an alloy grows weary and a groove wears away. Once she made technician she earned the right to go down into the pit alone, a hand crank for emergencies hooked to her belt. Later they handed her the hard diagnoses, the ones her colleagues had given up on. She listens first, palm flat on the frame, and names the guilty part before the housing is even open. Now she trains apprentices, and tells them the ear comes before the tool.

units: the laptop under review weakens as soon as the load runs on
the fault comes from the shape of the device
a powerful processor sits under a very thin lid
the heat pipe has only a small cross section
the heat piles up against the electronic board
the controller pulls the clock down to keep the chip safe
the fan grows loud and the compute speed drops
the keyboard turns warm and long stretches of typing suffer
a perforated stand improves the airflow without removing the cause
a thicker case would give better output for the same money
text: This ultrathin laptop falls apart as soon as the load runs longer than a handful of seconds, and the reason sits entirely in its shape. The maker dropped a generous processor under a lid pared down past sense, which leaves the heat pipe a laughable cross section. With nowhere to go, the heat piles up against the board, and the controller pulls the clock down at once to keep the silicon safe. You hear the result as clearly as you measure it: the fan climbs into a whine, compute speed sheds a third, then wanders without settling. The keyboard turns warm under the fingers, which spoils any long stretch of typing. Set the thing on a perforated stand and you buy some airflow and push the drop back, though the cause stays where it was. For the same money, a thicker case delivers more.
